rule.docs:
Summary

- Name: useImportExtensions
- Fix: safe
- Default severity: warn
- Available from version: 1.8.0
- Diagnostic category: lint/correctness/useImportExtensions

Domains

- Name: project


Description

 Enforce file extensions for relative imports.

 Browsers, Deno, and Node.js do not natively support importing files
 without extensions from JavaScript modules. This rule enforces the use
 of file extensions for relative imports to make the code more
 consistent -- and correct.

 In some cases, tooling can also benefit from explicit file extensions,
 because they do not need to guess which file to resolve.

 The rule checks both static imports (`import ... from "..."`) as well as
 dynamic imports such as `import(...)` and `require(...)`.

Examples

Invalid

 The following examples assume these imports will resolve to a file with
 an extension. Imports that don't resolve at all will not trigger a
 diagnostic.

 ```js
 import "./foo";
 ```
 ```js
 import "./foo/";
 ```
 ```js
 import "../";
 ```
 ```js
 import "../.";
 ```
 ```js
 import("./foo");
 ```
 ```js
 require("./foo");
 ```

Valid

 ```js
 import "biome";
 ```
 ```js
 import "./foo.js";
 ```
 ```js
 import "./bar/index.js";
 ```
 ```js
 import("./foo.js");
 ```
 ```js
 require("./foo.js");
 ```

Options

 The rule provides the options described below.

extensionMappings

 A map of file extensions to their suggested replacements. This allows you
 to specify custom mappings for import extensions. For example, you can
 map TypeScript imports to JavaScript extensions.

 This is useful if you are bundling your code to JavaScript into a package
 and want to make sure all imports of TypeScript files use the `.js` extension
 instead.

 If no mapping is found for a given extension, and the import is missing an extension,
 the rule will suggest using the actual extension of the resolved file.

 Default: `{}` (empty object)

 ```json,options
 {
     "options": {
         "extensionMappings": {
             "ts": "js",
             "tsx": "js"
         }
     }
 }
 ```

forceJsExtensions

 Normally, this rule suggests to use the extension of the module that is
 found in your project. For instance, `.ts` or `.tsx` for a TypeScript
 file. If this option is set to `true`, the rule will always suggest to
 use `.js` regardless of the extension in your project.

 This is useful if you use the `"module": "node16"` setting when building
 your code with `tsc`.

 Default: `false`

 ```json,options
 {
     "options": {
         "forceJsExtensions": true
     }
 }
 ```

Editor Configuration

 If you use Visual Studio Code, you can ensure that it adds the file
 extension when automatically importing a variable by configuring
 `javascript.preferences.importModuleSpecifierEnding` and
 `typescript.preferences.importModuleSpecifierEnding`
 in your [settings](https://code.visualstudio.com/docs/getstarted/settings).

analysis.summary: Flags relative imports missing file extensions.
analysis.fixDescription: Adds the file extension of the resolved target file; if forceJsExtensions is true, uses .js; otherwise uses the actual extension (.ts, .jsx, etc.) based on extensionMappings or filesystem resolution.
hazards: Rewriting `import "./dir"` to `import "./dir.js"` fails if `./dir` is a directory with an index file, changing the resolved module.
If the import points to a file without an extension (e.g., `import "./data"` where `./data` exists), adding `.js` may point to a non-existent file, causing a runtime error.

In projects with `extensionMappings` like {"ts": "js"}, rewriting `import "./foo.ts"` to `import "./foo.js"` assumes the bundled output uses .js, but if the file isn't actually emitted as .js, the import breaks.
When `forceJsExtensions: true`, rewriting `import "./component.jsx"` to `import "./component.js"` may fail if the bundler expects .jsx and does not map .js to JSX parsing.
The fix may drop inline comments attached to the import statement (e.g., `import "./foo" // init`) because the literal is replaced and comments are not reattached.
If the import is inside a conditional block (e.g., `if (true) import "./mod"`), the rewritten static import may be hoisted, altering execution timing relative to side effects.
Dynamic imports like `import(`locale/${lang}`)` are not flagged by this rule, but if mistakenly rewritten due to overbroad matching, it would break interpolation and cause syntax errors.

In ES modules, changing `import "./lib"` to `import "./lib.js"` may alter how the module is cached if another import refers to the same file via a different path (e.g., symlink), leading to duplicate execution.
If the resolved file is a .mjs file, the fix may incorrectly suggest .js instead of .mjs, breaking module type expectations in Node.js.
When the import uses a URL (e.g., `import "./foo?query"`), the fix naively appends .js, corrupting the URL and causing a fetch failure.
